passage:
I'm Harsha, and I used to sit with Avni every day at lunch. We shared pencils and made-up names. This year she made new friends in the football group, and I made mine in the art club. We still say hi, but we don't save each other seats.
Last week I saw her laughing with the football girls and felt a sad ache, like I had left something behind. I felt disloyal too, as if it was my fault. I told Mummy. She said it's okay to be sad when a friendship changes. That night I drew two chairs at a lunch table, and I left one of them empty.

qa.q: Which group did Avni make new friends in?
qa.a: Avni made new friends in the football group.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when seeing Avni laugh with the football girls?
qa.a: Harsha felt sad, with an ache, and disloyal, as if it was Harsha's fault.

qa.q: What helped Harsha begin to move on?
qa.a: Harsha told Mummy, who said it is okay to be sad when a friendship changes. Drawing two chairs, one empty, also gave the sadness a place to go.

qa.q: How might Avni see the change between herself and Harsha?
qa.a: Avni may see it as a natural drifting toward different friends and may not realise Harsha feels sad about it.

grounding: A child who drifted from a close friend feels sad and disloyal, and space to mourn helps.

passage:
Note by Uday, Class 4 teacher.
Zeenat has been quiet for two weeks. Her old friend Meher now sits with the football group, and the two no longer share a desk. At art period Zeenat drew two girls on a bench with a gap between them and would not colour the gap.
I didn't tell her to find new friends. I said, "It's sad when a friend grows in a different direction. You can miss her and not be angry." Zeenat's eyes filled. I let her stay with the paints for the rest of the period. I've asked her mother to keep an ear open at home, and I'll check in with Zeenat again on Friday.
— Uday

qa.q: What did Zeenat draw at art period?
qa.a: Zeenat drew two girls on a bench with a gap between them.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she would not colour the gap?
qa.a: Zeenat was sad and missing Meher, as her quiet weeks, the drawing and her filling eyes show.

qa.q: What did Uday do that gave Zeenat room to mourn?
qa.a: Uday did not tell her to find new friends. Uday said she could miss Meher without being angry, let her stay with the paints and planned a check-in on Friday.

qa.q: How might Meher see the change in the friendship?
qa.a: Meher may see it as a natural change toward the football group and may not know Zeenat is grieving.

grounding: A child who has drifted from a close friend feels sad and disloyal; space to mourn the change helps her move on.

passage: The school picnic bus was delayed an hour by the rain, and everyone was stuck in the hot school hall. Binita saw Usha sitting alone by the window, and her stomach twisted. Last year they'd been inseparable, matching hairbands, the same seat on every trip. This year Binita had joined the football team, and her lunch table had changed. Usha had drifted to the art club. They hadn't argued. They just talked less, then barely. When the bus finally came, Binita sat with her new teammates and felt like a traitor all the way to the lake. That evening she told her mother, "I'm a bad friend." Her mother sat with her. "You're not bad. Friendships change sometimes. It's okay to feel sad about it." Binita cried a little. The next week, she waved to Usha in the corridor. Usha waved back, smiling.

qa.q: What did Binita join this year?
qa.a: The football team.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling on the bus to the lake?
qa.a: She felt sad and guilty, like a traitor, for sitting with her new friends instead of Usha.

qa.q: How did Binita's mother help her?
qa.a: She gave Binita space to feel sad and explained that friendships sometimes change, so Binita didn't have to feel bad about it.

qa.q: How might Usha see the friendship now?
qa.a: Usha seems to accept the change too, smiling and waving back when Binita greeted her.

grounding: Shows a child who has drifted from a close friend feeling sad and disloyal, and being given space to mourn it.

passage: For three years Baljeet and Kavitha walked home together from school in their Chandigarh sector, sharing a packet of peanuts every day. This year Kavitha moved to the other section, made new friends and started taking the bus. Baljeet still walked. At first they met at the gate. Then less. Then not at all. One afternoon Baljeet saw Kavitha laughing with her new group and felt a pang so sharp she had to stop walking. At home she sat on the stairs and didn't eat. "It feels like I lost her," she told Dadi. Dadi gave her a peanut and said, "You did lose something. It's okay to miss it. You'll both carry those walks with you." Baljeet cried, and felt lighter afterwards. The next week, she started walking home with a girl from her own section.

qa.q: What did Baljeet and Kavitha share every day on their walk home?
qa.a: A packet of peanuts.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when she saw Kavitha laughing with her new group?
qa.a: She felt a sharp pang of sadness and loss, as if she had lost her friend.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that helped Baljeet move on?
qa.a: She agreed that Baljeet had lost something and said it was okay to miss it, giving her space to mourn.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel about the change?
qa.a: Kavitha may not even realise how much Baljeet misses her, since she's busy with her new friends and bus rides.

grounding: Shows a child who drifted from a close friend feeling sad and lost, and a grandmother giving her space to mourn so she can move on.

passage:
"Jeevan, wait up."
Jeevan turned at the school gate. Naveen was running to catch up, backpack bouncing.
"Hi," said Jeevan. It felt awkward.
"We don't really hang out anymore, huh," said Naveen.
"Yeah. You've got cricket, I've got chess club."
"I feel bad about it."
"Me too. Like I did something wrong."
"Did you?"
Jeevan thought. "No. We just like different things now."
Naveen kicked a stone. "It's sad though."
"It is sad." Jeevan swallowed. "You were my best friend in Class 3."
"You were mine."
They stood quietly. Then Naveen grinned. "Remember the frog in the water tank?"
Jeevan laughed. "Mrs. Rao screamed."
"Okay. See you around?"
"See you around." Jeevan walked home slowly, sad but somehow lighter.

qa.q: What club does Jeevan go to?
qa.a: Chess club.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel walking home?
qa.a: Jeevan felt sad but somehow lighter after talking honestly with Naveen.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan and Naveen let go of their old closeness?
qa.a: Saying out loud that it was sad and remembering the frog story together gave them space to mourn the friendship without blame.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about drifting apart?
qa.a: Naveen felt bad and a bit sad, but was also relieved to talk about it.

grounding: Shows a child who has drifted from a close friend feeling sad and disloyal, and a shared honest goodbye helping both move on.

passage: In Class 3, Hrithik and I did everything together. I'm Indu. We shared a bench, swapped tiffins, and had a secret handshake with seven parts. This year he joined the cricket group and I joined drama, and slowly we stopped sitting together. One day I saw him laughing with Aman at our old bench, and I felt sad and also bad, like I had broken a promise, even though nobody had. At home I cried a bit. Mumma said, "It's okay to miss him. Friendships change shape." She didn't tell me to cheer up. I did our handshake alone in my room, all seven parts, and then I felt a little lighter. Now we say hi in the corridor. It's different. It's okay.

qa.q: How many parts did Indu and Hrithik's secret handshake have?
qa.a: It had seven parts.

qa.q: What did Indu feel on seeing Hrithik laughing at their old bench?
qa.a: Indu felt sad and guilty, as if a promise had been broken, even though nobody had broken one.

qa.q: What helped Indu move on?
qa.a: Mumma letting Indu miss Hrithik without saying cheer up, and doing the handshake one last time as a small goodbye.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel about the friendship now?
qa.a: He may feel a little wistful too but happy in cricket, since he still says hi in the corridor.

grounding: Shows a child who drifted from a close friend feeling sad and disloyal, and space to mourn helping the child move on.
